title: Supreme Court Blocks Trump's Mail Ballot Restrictions Before Midterms
summary:
The Supreme Court on Monday rejected President Donald Trump's bid to restrict mail ballots for the midterm elections, capping a flurry of last-minute legal action with voting already underway. The decision allows states to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes they've used for years — systems that have accounted for nearly a third of votes cast.

It was a stark defeat for Trump on an issue he has consistently emphasized as vital to ensuring election integrity, even though there is virtually no evidence of fraud with mail ballots. The Supreme Court majority did not detail its reasoning, as is typical for its emergency docket. Two justices, Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, publicly dissented.

The Trump administration had asked the court to clear the way for restrictions before the pivotal November contests for control of Congress. Alito wrote in his dissent that the Postal Service "has broad authority to regulate the mail" and likely does have the power to enforce Trump's restrictions. Justice Brett Kavanaugh agreed that the restrictions should not go into effect for the midterms but indicated he might rule in favor of the administration if the issue returns to the court later.

Election officials have said there was simply no way to carry out a complete overhaul in the weeks before the midterms. Indeed, Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin began sending mail ballots to voters over the past week while the new system was still not active. The administration's efforts had the potential to be especially disruptive in states like Washington and Oregon that send out ballots entirely by mail.

"Washington's election workers are already hard at work preparing to carry out a safe, secure, and accurate election," Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said in a written statement. "Now, that work continues without having to upend our election processes to meet unrealistic ballot mail requirements." In Colorado, Secretary of State Jena Griswold called the ruling "a major victory for Colorado and American democracy."

The administration's plan would have required states to adopt a uniform envelope style and submit lists of eligible voters to an online portal. The Postal Service could refuse to deliver ballots to states that didn't comply. A whistleblower report said the postal system's requirements could lead to millions of mail ballots never being sent because the portal wasn't properly built and a single bar code error could result in an entire batch of ballots being tossed out.

Democratic state officials and voting rights groups challenged the restrictions in court, arguing that the president has no constitutional authority to set election rules that would "virtually eliminate mail voting on the eve of a major election." Lower courts agreed and blocked Trump's plan. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
why_it_matters: This case is about who gets to write the rules for voting — the president, the states, or Congress — and it will shape how millions of Americans, including students who will soon be old enough to vote, cast their ballots. It also shows how quickly the Supreme Court can change election rules without giving a full explanation.

background_read: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States; its nine justices have the final say on whether laws and government actions follow the Constitution.

In the U.S., elections are run by the states, not by the president — the Constitution gives state legislatures the main power to set voting rules, though Congress can pass laws that override them. President Donald Trump (the U.S. president since 2025) has argued the federal government should have more say over how ballots are handled.

Voting by mail is not new: soldiers cast mail ballots during the Civil War, and Oregon became the first state to run all of its elections by mail, with Washington and later Colorado and others following. Mail voting surged during the COVID-19 pandemic and now regularly accounts for a large share of ballots.
The U.S. Postal Service (the government agency that delivers the mail) is controlled by the executive branch, which is why a president's appointees can shape how ballots move through it.

The justices decided this case on the 'emergency docket' — sometimes called the 'shadow docket' — where the court acts fast, often without explaining its reasoning, which leaves the legal rules unsettled for the next case.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — state election officials and voting-rights groups
perspectives.description: Officials like Washington's Steve Hobbs and Colorado's Jena Griswold see the ruling as a win because it lets them keep using systems they have tested for years, with ballots already going out. Voting-rights groups argued that changing the rules weeks before an election would have disenfranchised voters, so they read the decision as protecting access to the ballot.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — the administration and the dissenting justices
perspectives.description: Alito wrote that the Postal Service has broad authority over the mail, and Kavanaugh hinted he might side with the administration in a future case. From this view, uniform federal rules are needed to prevent fraud — even though the article notes there is virtually no evidence of fraud with mail ballots — and the court's unexplained emergency rulings leave big questions about presidential power unanswered.

The case fits a pattern: the Supreme Court's emergency docket decides fast, often without explaining its reasoning, so the underlying question of how much power a president has over election mail stays unsettled. Historically, states run elections while Congress sets federal rules, and this fight is about where that boundary sits.

Kavanaugh's opinion is a signal that the issue could come back after the midterms, when there is more time to argue it fully. Meanwhile, states and the Postal Service still have to agree on how ballots move through the mail, and any future ruling could force those systems to change again.
